tldr: An innovative framework that solves unseen humanoid loco-manipulation tasks by evolving staged reward programs at test time through LLM and simulation trial-and-error—all without retraining the pre-trained controller at all.
hero_caption: The concept of InterEvolve. When given a task outside its training data—rotating a box in place—a fixed whole-body controller trained only on lifting and carrying boxes fails under human-designed rewards. In contrast, the reward program evolved by InterEvolve generates a novel whole-body strategy that uses the body to pull the box closer and succeeds.
overview:
Enabling humanoid robots to perform diverse whole-body loco-manipulation tasks typically required retraining reinforcement learning (RL) policies from scratch for every new task. However, controllers pre-trained on large-scale human demonstration data already possess the latent motor competence needed to solve unseen tasks. The real challenge has been finding a way to tap into that latent competence.

To address this, the authors propose InterEvolve, an approach that evolves task specifications as "reward programs" at test time instead of retraining the controller itself. In this framework, an LLM agent writes multi-stage reward programs, a numerical optimizer (CMA-ES) fine-tunes their continuous constants, and candidate programs are repeatedly verified across parallel simulation rollouts. Furthermore, by adopting an object-aware forward-backward (FB) behavioral foundation model as the controller—which instantly projects any reward into a latent prompt—the system executes new rewards with zero additional policy training.

In evaluation across 8 task families, including box carrying, obstacle avoidance, box tipping, and kicking, InterEvolve more than doubled the success rate compared to fixed human-designed rewards, discovering novel contact strategies autonomously. In addition, by reusing previously successful programs as a "skill library," the system effortlessly solved long-horizon composite tasks and operated fully autonomously on a physical Unitree G1 robot using onboard camera perception.
contributions: Established an adaptation framework that unlocks the latent competence of whole-body controllers via test-time computation (LLM and simulation trial-and-error) without any policy retraining.

Developed an object-aware forward-backward (FB) behavioral foundation model that attaches an object residual module to a frozen body prior, turning arbitrary rewards into whole-body object interactions zero-shot.
Proposed an efficient bi-level evolution mechanism combining logical structural revisions by an LLM with continuous parameter optimization via CMA-ES.
Demonstrated long-horizon composite task completion and fully autonomous deployment on a physical humanoid (Unitree G1) by accumulating and reusing solved task programs in a skill library.

sections.heading: How can we unlock unseen tasks without retraining the controller?
sections.summary: Humanoid controllers trained on large datasets hold rich latent competence, but they fail out-of-the-box on new tasks outside their training data. This paper introduces a new framework that keeps the controller weights frozen and evolves reward programs at test time to solve tasks.
sections.details:
Recent humanoid controllers trained on human motion data can perform rich movements like pushing, lifting, and carrying boxes. However, when faced with an unseen task—such as tipping a box onto a different face—they fail if that specific demonstration was absent from the training data. The key insight here is that the motor coordination required to tip a box already lies dormant within what the controller can do.

Conventional approaches either provide target trajectories or retrain policies using reinforcement learning (RL) for every single task. However, designing detailed reference trajectories by hand is notoriously difficult in complex manipulation tasks where contact modes shift frequently. Furthermore, running an RL training loop every time a reward is tweaked costs immense computation time and overhead.

This study introduces InterEvolve, bringing the concept of LLM test-time scaling—using more compute at inference time for deliberate search and reflection—into robot control. Tasks are specified as programs comprising staged rewards and completion conditions. Without updating the controller weights at all, an LLM evolves the program structure based on execution feedback from simulation. Successfully solved tasks are then recorded in a skill library and reused for future, more complex tasks.

sections.heading: Loco-manipulation, behavioral foundation models, and automated reward design
sections.summary: The paper contextualizes prior work across humanoid loco-manipulation, behavioral foundation models that decompose successor measures, and LLM-based code generation and reward design. InterEvolve stands out by searching task specifications directly via test-time compute without policy retraining.
sections.details:
This work builds upon three main research threads:

- **Humanoid Loco-Manipulation**
  Recent years have seen rapid progress in learning whole-body loco-manipulation through imitation learning and RL, transferring these policies to real humanoids. However, many existing approaches remain restricted to tracking human reference motions or sequencing predefined skills with high-level planners, limiting flexible adaptation to unseen contact modes.

- **Behavioral Foundation Models and Reward Inference**
  Using Forward-Backward (FB) representations that decompose successor state occupancy, any reward function can be projected into a latent prompt, eliciting the corresponding behavior from a single policy without retraining. However, previous humanoid FB models (like BFM-Zero) only observed the robot's own body state, suffering from a severe limitation: behaviors collapsed to identical motions regardless of object state variations.

- **LLM-Based Reward Design and Test-Time Search**
  Using LLMs to write RL reward functions (such as Eureka) has attracted significant attention, but evaluating each reward candidate required running a full RL training loop, taking hours or days per iteration. InterEvolve evaluates programs simply by rolling them out on a frozen FB model in parallel simulation, achieving an exceptionally fast feedback loop.

sections.heading: How InterEvolve works: evolving reward programs with an object-aware FB model
sections.summary: Tasks are formulated as multi-stage reward programs and executed instantly by an FB foundation model equipped with object observations. The search operates as a bi-level loop: LLM structural revision on the outside and CMA-ES constant tuning on the inside.
sections.details:
The overall architecture of InterEvolve forms a pipeline that represents task specifications as editable strategies, evaluating and evolving them iteratively.

### 3.1 Problem Formulation
A task is specified by a natural language instruction $\ell$ (e.g., "kick the box to the target mark using only your feet") and a scene context $c$ (obstacle and object positions). A verifier $\mathcal{C}$ comprises multiple binary criteria $C_i$ (e.g., do not fall, do not use hands, reach target position). Once parsed from the task by an LLM, the verifier remains fixed. This prevents the agent from trivializing the task by stealthily relaxing success conditions.

### 3.2 Reward Programs as Editable Strategies
A strategy is formulated as a program $P= ig( oldsymbol{	heta}, \{(r_j, g_j)\}_{j=1}^J ig)$. Each stage $j$ consists of a reward function code $r_j$ and a transition condition $g_j$, parameterized by tunable continuous constants $ oldsymbol{	heta}$ such as weights and thresholds. Explicitly separating stages—such as approaching an object, making contact to push, and retreating—makes it much easier for the LLM to diagnose exactly which stage failed.

### 3.3 Zero-Retraining Reward Execution via an Object-Aware FB Model
To execute reward programs, an FB (Forward-Backward) behavioral foundation model serves as the controller $\pi$. Any reward $r$ is evaluated over a fixed bank of pre-collected body-object states $\mathcal{B}$ and instantly projected into a latent prompt $ oldsymbol{z}$.
A key innovation here is making the model object-aware. While keeping the body network of a prior humanoid model (BFM-Zero) frozen, the authors attach a learnable object residual module that reads relative object positions, orientations, velocities, and displacement vectors from robot links to the object's surface. This allows the robot to manipulate objects deliberately without compromising its whole-body balance and stability.

### 3.4 Bi-Level Evolution of Reward Programs
Program optimization is carried out across two distinct loops:
- **Outer Loop (LLM Structural Revision)**: The LLM agent inspects execution feedback provided in the prompt (e.g., failure rates per criterion, stages where execution stalled) and proposes structural edits—such as adding/removing stages or rewriting reward terms—via in-context learning.
- **Inner Loop (CMA-ES Numerical Tuning)**: For the structure proposed by the LLM, the CMA-ES evolutionary algorithm automatically optimizes the continuous constants $ oldsymbol{	heta}$, including weights and thresholds.
Candidate programs are evaluated across parallel simulation environments and accepted only if they statistically outperform the current best program. Successfully verified programs are logged into a skill library $\mathcal{H}$ to be referenced in subsequent tasks.

captions.F2: System overview of InterEvolve. (a) An LLM generates staged reward programs while referencing a skill library. (b) The object-aware FB model computes rewards over a state bank and projects them into latent prompts, executing the controller without retraining. (c) Verification results across parallel environments are fed back into inner-loop constant tuning via CMA-ES and outer-loop structural revision via the LLM.

sections.heading: Surprising adaptability: doubling human reward success and deploying to hardware
sections.summary: Evaluated across 8 task families, programs evolved by InterEvolve achieved more than double the success rate of human-designed rewards. Stored skills enabled long-horizon composite tasks, and skills transferred directly to a physical Unitree G1 robot for autonomous execution.
sections.details:
The proposed approach was evaluated in simulation (Isaac Lab) and on a physical humanoid robot (Unitree G1).

### 4.1 Experimental Setup and Baselines
The FB model was pre-trained on large-scale human-object interaction datasets (OMOMO, GRAB). The robot platform used was the Unitree G1 (equipped with rubber wrists and Inspire 5-finger dexterous hands). The evaluation suite covered 8 task families, including pushing to a mark, carrying at various heights, tipping a box onto a face, foot-only manipulation (kicking), lifting onto a table, and navigating gates and obstacles. Comparisons were made against a dedicated tracking model (ULTRA), a body-only FB model (BFM-Zero), human-engineered programs, and initial LLM proposals.

### 4.2 Effectiveness in Reference Motion Tracking
In reference trajectory tracking tasks, the object-aware FB model achieved performance close to that of the tracking specialist (ULTRA). Furthermore, when the agent was tasked with designing a reward term to counteract drift in world coordinates, tracking error dropped significantly, surpassing ULTRA's success rate.

### 4.3 General Task Completion via Reward Program Evolution
In tasks where no reference motions were provided and only completion criteria were given, human-designed reward programs (even after CMA-ES tuning) achieved an average success rate of roughly 27%. In contrast, InterEvolve achieved over 58%—more than double the performance.
Ablation studies highlighted several key findings:
- **Importance of Staged Rewards**: Restricting programs to a single stage caused the largest drop in performance. In contact-rich tasks, breaking goals into stages is indispensable.
- **Role of Numerical Tuning**: Omitting CMA-ES constant tuning caused even structurally sound programs to fail due to weight imbalances.
- **Benefits of Test-Time Computation**: Earned verification tiers increased monotonically over successive rounds, and the robot discovered unexpected, emergent strategies, such as hooking its foot on a box corner to spin it.

### 4.4 Skill Reuse and Real-Robot Deployment
Storing previously discovered programs in the skill library dramatically improved performance on long-horizon composite tasks, such as table-to-table object transfer, box stacking, and carry-place-and-kick sequences (achieving roughly 50% success on tasks where the baseline without a library scored near 0%). Furthermore, a long-horizon task requiring the robot to sequentially arrange 6 scattered boxes into a ring was completed by a single controller without resets.
Finally, programs evolved in simulation transferred directly to a physical Unitree G1 robot. Relying solely on object pose estimation (FoundationPose) from an onboard head camera, the robot achieved fully autonomous pushing and kicking behaviors.

captions.F3: Dexterous manipulation and long-horizon skill composition. (a) A G1 robot equipped with Inspire 5-finger hands stably grasps and lifts a small bottle using a calibrated reward. (b) Chaining evolved pushing and walking skills allows the robot to seamlessly arrange 6 scattered boxes along a specified circle without interruption.
captions.F4: Fully autonomous execution on a physical Unitree G1 robot. Programs evolved in simulation are deployed directly to the hardware. Using onboard RGB-D camera feeds and FoundationPose for object pose estimation, the robot robustly executes box kicking (top row) and pushing (bottom row).

sections.heading: A new division of labor between intelligence and whole-body control
sections.summary: This work introduces a paradigm that clearly separates low-level motor control from high-level task reasoning. Much like test-time reasoning in language models, robots can now self-evolve by deliberating and experimenting with execution outcomes at test time.
sections.details:
InterEvolve demonstrates a new division of labor for humanoid intelligence. The behavioral foundation model learns basic motor competence once at scale, and its weights remain frozen. In contrast, task-specific knowledge—determining what to achieve and how—is maintained outside the model weights as inspectable, reusable reward program code.

This architecture enables evolution at two distinct timescales. The controller is strengthened slowly and thoroughly via larger interaction datasets, while the LLM agent grows smarter rapidly through test-time search and skill accumulation. Neither forces the other to retrain.

Moreover, because physical simulation feedback grounds the agent's reasoning in the physical world, its outputs avoid language hallucination and converge on executable, robust strategies. This highlights a promising future where scaling test-time compute empowers robots to autonomously enhance their problem-solving capabilities.

sections.heading: Appendix: Implementation details of the object-aware FB model and reward search
sections.summary: Details regarding the controller residual architecture, state bank sampling methods, the reward-tilted aggregation mechanism, and prompt designs provided to the LLM.
sections.details:
The appendix provides technical details omitted from the main text.

### A. Object-Aware Module Design
In addition to the object's position, orientation, and velocity, the state features input to the residual module include displacement vectors from 30 link locations on the robot (54 locations when using 5-finger hands) to the nearest points on the object's surface. These represent proximity rather than contact forces, acting as residuals on top of the frozen body prior. Ablation experiments confirm that omitting these surface displacement vectors causes object tracking error to spike.

### B. Reward Inference and "Reward-Tilted" Aggregation
The state bank $\mathcal{B}$ consists of thousands to tens of thousands of states sampled from training replay buffers and remains fixed during search. When mapping rewards into latent prompts $ oldsymbol{z}$, instead of a simple average, the method uses reward-tilted aggregation weighted by a coefficient $ eta$. This strongly concentrates the prompt on high-reward states, even for behaviors that appear rarely in the training data, such as kicking.

### C. Prompts and Learning from Failures
Rather than simply telling the LLM agent that an attempt failed, the prompt provides detailed statistical summaries across 192 parallel environments, including failure percentages per verification criterion and whether the failure stems from variance or a flawed median. This allows the agent to distinguish between an unlucky outlier and a broken strategy, guiding it to write precise, effective code revisions.

captions.F7: Evolution of reward programs for the kicking task. In the initial proposal (top row), the foot misses the box entirely. Over successive rounds, the agent introduces revisions such as taking a run-up before swinging the leg and maintaining balance without using hands, ultimately arriving at an effective kicking strategy in the final round (bottom row).
captions.F9: Three long-horizon composite tasks achieved using the skill library. Top: lifting, carrying, and placing an object between tables. Middle: lifting and stacking two boxes. Bottom: carrying a box, placing it on the floor, and kicking it forward. All are executed using the exact same underlying controller.

takeaways: Unseen contact-rich manipulation tasks can be solved without retraining policy weights by combining an expressive behavioral foundation model with test-time reward evolution.
Decomposing tasks into staged reward programs and separating structural exploration (LLM) from parameter tuning (CMA-ES) is crucial for mastering contact-rich interactions.
Accumulating verified reward programs as text-based assets in a skill library dramatically slashes the search cost of solving long-horizon composite tasks from scratch.
limitations: It cannot unlock motor skills that exceed the controller's underlying physical capabilities if those dynamics were never encountered during foundation model pre-training.

Because each search round requires parallel simulation rollouts, solving a single task demands several GPU hours and incurs LLM inference delays, preventing real-time, instantaneous online adaptation during physical execution.

Newly acquired skills and knowledge at test time are stored solely as external reward program code, with no mechanism to backpropagate or distill them into the neural network weights of the low-level controller.
